STEGANOGRAPHY author: Slender-man

Case 01: Tones


After his request for a salary raise was refused, an employee was flagged for suspicious activity over the past two weeks. A dedicated camera with audio recording was installed in his office. The only usable footage is a stretch of what appears to be ordinary office ambience. Find out what was really going on.

Exhibit: office_cam_audio.wav · Flag format: UNINTENDED{...}







Listen before you touch anything


The case ships as one exhibit, office_cam_audio.wav. Played back, it is mostly silence and room noise, but there are short bursts that sound exactly like someone pressing keys on a telephone . Those keypad tones are  encoding. Nobody hides ordinary ambience in a phone dialer, so the “office noise” is a message.


Why this path: keypad tones are one of the most recognisable audio signatures. Instead of burning time on spectrograms or LSB tricks in the , I went straight to a DTMF decoder: dtmf.netlify.app.








Feed the evidence to the machine


I uploaded the file and left the sensitivity threshold at its default of 0.050. The decoder ran almost instantly.


The timeline tells the story: silence from second 1 to 8, then dense bursts of keypad digits from second 9 to 29, then silence again. Someone dialed a long string into that office.








Read the string, then cook it


At the bottom sits the line we came for, right after the word “Decoded”:

85#78#73#78#84#69#78#68#69#68#123#52#84#84#51#110#116#49#48#110#95#116#48#95#100#51#116#52#49#108#53#125

Numbers separated by #, all between roughly 48 and 125 and starting with 85, 78, 73. That range is exactly where printable  lives, so each number is one character. For this I opened  (gchq.github.io/CyberChef), pasted the string into the input and chose the recipe From Decimal with the delimiter on Auto, so it detects the # by itself.


Why this path: a decoder that outputs plain digits with one repeated separator is almost always one transform away from text. CyberChef does that transform in one click, with no script needed.


And with one click on bake, the site cooked the flag for us.

CASE CLOSED

Conclusion


The employee never said a word. He dialed his message into the room and let the camera record it as background noise. The whole case turned on one habit: treating something that sounds boring as suspect.


    

  • Identify the signal first. Phone-keypad beeps mean . Naming the encoding at the first listen saved me from trying every audio stego trick in the book.
    • 

  • Match the decoder to the evidence. A dedicated DTMF decoder gave me the digits in seconds. A spectrogram could only have confirmed that tones were present; it cannot hand you the digits, so the decoder was the right tool.
    • 

  • Read the shape of the output. Numbers split by a repeated separator, in the printable range, are almost always  codes. Spotting that told me exactly which recipe to use.
    • 

  • Chain simple tools. Two common, free tools solved the case. The flag, attention to details, is also good advice for any investigation.


dtmf.netlify.appCyberChefFrom Decimal
